title: Found in Conversation: LLMs Teach Themselves to Close the Multi-Turn Gap
claim: A two-stage procedure first warm-starts a model on constructed multi-turn data, then distills single-turn teacher behavior into the multi-turn student.
layout: 2 stacked stages, left-to-right flow, numbered steps in Stage 1, teacher/student views in Stage 2
description: Two stacked rounded panels with blue and purple outlines. The top panel, Stage 1 (SFT), has three numbered steps flowing left to right. Step 1 shows a single-turn math word problem going through an LLM robot icon (sharding) into multi-turn shards u1..uN. Step 2 is a grid of generic versus specific, question-style versus statement-style deferral turns, with a final complete-turn answer below it. Step 3 shows a frozen backbone feeding a LoRA adapter, trained with an SFT loss. The bottom panel, Stage 2 (VASD), puts the teacher view (the single-turn prompt) on the left and the student view (an interleaved u/m multi-turn chain) on the right. Both share one backbone, and a dashed arrow leads to the final answer turn. A bracket below leads to the J-S divergence loss.
caption: Overview of FOUND IN CONVERSATION. SFT warm-starts the model: build a multi-turn corpus from a standard single-turn benchmark, construct per-turn gold answers with diversity, and train with a standard causal-LM loss. VASD runs the same backbone on two information-equivalent views: a teacher view on the single-turn setting and a student view on the multi-turn setting with intermediate responses sampled on-policy. A token-level distillation loss aligns the student to the teacher.
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) interactions are typically underspecified, with users clarifying all necessary details across multiple conversational turns. Yet recent work shows that LLMs perform far worse in this multi-turn setting than in a single turn with the same information available at once, a phenomenon termed "Lost-in-Conversation." However, bridging this gap effectively remains an open problem. Here we introduce Found in Conversation (FiC), a training framework where a model teaches itself to find and recover its single-turn competence given underspecified multi-turn prompts. We develop View-Asymmetric Self-Distillation, which distills across two views of the same task information (a single-turn view for the teacher and a multi-turn view for the student), transferring strong single-turn behavior into weak multi-turn behavior. This requires no stronger external teacher, which is unavailable as even frontier LLMs exhibit this gap. Across model families (Llama, Qwen, Phi, and OLMo) and sizes (3B-14B), FiC attains 92-100% of single-turn performance, yielding more efficient and helpful multi-turn conversations with single-turn capabilities largely intact.
